title: Saul Rescues Jabesh-gilead
summary: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and offers to make a treaty only if he can gouge out the right eye of every man in the city. The elders of Jabesh send for help, and when the news reaches Gibeah, the Spirit of God rushes upon Saul. He summons Israel by sending pieces of a slaughtered yoke of oxen through the land, musters a great army, and routs the Ammonites in a dawn attack. Saul refuses to execute those who had despised him, and the people go to Gilgal to confirm him as king.
story: Chapter 10 ended with Saul chosen as king but despised by some who asked how this man could save them. Chapter 11 answers them. Saul, still working his father's fields, receives the Spirit and does exactly what Israel wanted a king to do: he goes out before them and fights their battles. It is the high point of Saul's career and his most attractive moment, marked by courage, decisive action, and mercy toward his critics. The chapter ends with the kingdom renewed at Gilgal, which leads into Samuel's farewell speech in chapter 12. The reader who knows how Saul's story ends will feel the weight of this bright beginning.
historical:
The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan River, with their capital at Rabbah (modern Amman, in Jordan). They were a recurring enemy of Israel, especially over the land of Gilead, the hilly region east of the Jordan where the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh had settled. Jabesh-gilead lay in northern Gilead, east of the Jordan. Its bond with Saul's tribe went back to Judges 21, where the surviving men of Benjamin took wives from Jabesh-gilead, so many Benjamites had kin there. The people of Jabesh will remember Saul's rescue: after his death, they travel through the night to recover his body from the walls of Beth-shan and bury it (31:11-13).

The Dead Sea Scroll manuscript known as 4QSamuel-a contains an extra paragraph before this chapter, not found in the standard Hebrew text, describing how Nahash had been oppressing the Gadites and Reubenites and gouging out their right eyes, and how some who escaped fled to Jabesh. Some modern translations include it; others do not, judging that it may be a later expansion. Its presence helps explain why Nahash was already at Jabesh. The large numbers in verse 8 raise the same question as other military figures in Samuel, whether thousand should be read as a literal count or as a military unit.
cultural:
A treaty (literally a covenant) between a stronger and a weaker party was a normal way of ending a siege in the ancient Near East; the weaker city would surrender and become a vassal. Nahash's condition, putting out every man's right eye, was designed as public humiliation, a reproach on all Israel, and it may also have been meant to make the men unfit for battle. The elders' request for seven days to seek a deliverer suggests that Nahash was confident no help would come, a mark of Israel's weakness without a unified leadership.

Saul's summons by sending pieces of oxen was a dramatic threat that anyone who did not come would suffer the same fate as the animals. Readers of Judges would remember a grim parallel: in Judges 19:29, after an atrocity committed at Gibeah, a Levite cut up his concubine's body and sent the pieces through Israel, which led to civil war. Saul, from that same town of Gibeah, uses a similar act to unite the tribes rather than divide them. The morning watch was the last of the three watches into which the night was divided, the hours just before dawn, a favorite time for surprise attacks.
literary: The chapter reads like one of the deliverance stories in Judges: an enemy oppresses, the people cry out, the Spirit of God rushes upon a leader, the leader musters Israel, and the enemy is defeated. Saul's first appearance is carefully staged. He comes in from the field, behind his oxen, like Gideon threshing wheat (Judges 6:11); he hears the news, the Spirit comes, and his anger burns. The pieces of oxen show him using the very animals he was driving. The resolution has two parts. After the battle, the people want to kill Saul's critics, and Saul refuses, crediting the LORD with the victory; the narrator presents this as Saul's finest moment. Then Samuel calls the people to renew the kingship at Gilgal, which brings the process that began in chapter 8 to completion.

outline.t: The Spirit comes on Saul, and Israel musters

doctrines.note: The Spirit of God rushes upon Saul and moves him to righteous anger and decisive action. As in the stories of the judges, the Spirit equips a leader for the task of delivering God's people. The victory is presented as the Spirit's work through Saul, not merely Saul's own courage.

Saul says, “today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel” (verse 13). In the Old Testament, salvation often means rescue from enemies and danger, and it is always ultimately God's work, even when a human leader is the instrument.

The chapter shows kingship at its best: a leader who serves the people, delivers the oppressed, and gives God the credit. Saul's mercy toward those who despised him shows the kind of ruler God's people need.

words.note: Teshu'ah, deliverance, salvation, victory. The messengers promise the men of Jabesh deliverance by the time the sun is hot, and Saul says the LORD has worked salvation in Israel. The word ties military rescue to God's saving action and is related to the name Joshua and, through it, to the name Jesus.

Chadash, to renew or restore. Samuel calls the people to renew the kingship at Gilgal. Scholars debate whether this means restoring something disputed after the grumbling of 10:27, confirming Saul publicly after his first victory, or a renewal of covenant commitment. In any case, the kingship is now established with the people's full support.

Berit, covenant or treaty. The men of Jabesh ask Nahash to make a covenant with them, meaning a surrender treaty. The word used for the LORD's relationship with Israel is here a treaty of submission to a cruel enemy, which highlights how desperate the situation was.

Pachad, dread or terror. The terror of the LORD fell on the people, and they came out as one man. The phrase describes an overwhelming awe sent by God, which moves Israel to act together. God is at work not only in Saul but in the people's response.

christ: Saul's rescue of Jabesh-gilead is a picture of what Israel hoped for in a king: someone anointed and empowered by God's Spirit to rescue the helpless from a cruel enemy. His refusal to take revenge on his critics also reflects the kind of mercy a righteous king should show. The New Testament presents Jesus as the anointed king in whom these hopes are realized, who rescues his people from powers they could not defeat and who shows mercy even to those who rejected him (Luke 23:34). The connection is thematic. Saul's story does not predict Christ, and Saul's reign will soon collapse, but this chapter shows the good that God intended kingship to accomplish, which the Bible sees completed only in Jesus.

hard.q: Why does Saul seem to become king three times, in chapters 10 and 11?
hard.a: Saul is anointed privately (10:1), chosen by lot at Mizpah (10:17-24), and then the people make him king at Gilgal (11:15), which can look like three different accounts of how he came to the throne. Many critical scholars see here several traditions about Saul's rise, some more favorable to kingship than others, gathered by the book's editors. Others read the steps as a coherent process that fits what is known of how leaders were recognized in the ancient world: private designation by God through a prophet, public selection before the tribes, and confirmation after the new leader proves himself in battle. Samuel himself calls the Gilgal event a renewal, which supports the idea of a staged process. Readers on both sides agree that the finished account presents Saul's kingship as coming from God, confirmed by the people, and proven in action.

questions: Saul's anger at the Ammonites' cruelty was stirred by the Spirit of God. What is the difference between righteous anger and ordinary anger, and when have you seen anger lead to good action?
After his victory Saul refused to punish those who had despised him. Why is mercy toward critics a mark of good leadership?
The people of Jabesh remembered Saul's rescue for the rest of his life. Who has come to your rescue, and how have you remembered it?
